title: Detection overlay on a real frame: is the detection right?
summary: A contour found by an algorithm drawn over the original image, with a scale bar. It lets you judge by eye whether the detected edge sits where the object's edge is.

media.alt: A grey image of a bright oval blob with an orange ragged contour drawn on its edge and a teal scale bar labelled 5 mm.
media.caption: Reference render with synthetic demonstration data (design-system gallery).

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: Is the detection right?
read_the_figure.axes: x and y: image coordinates (labelled px in the figure but ticked in normalised units, see below). Grey levels: recorded intensity. Orange: the detected contour. Teal bar: 5 mm scale.
look_at: Does the orange contour follow the visible edge of the bright region all the way round?
Where does the contour wobble or break? Noise gives a ragged contour.
Is the original image still visible inside and outside the contour?
What does the scale bar say about the size of the detected object?
read_the_figure.proves: A contour that lies on the visible edge of the object at all points shows that the segmentation found the right thing in this frame. It does not prove it does so in every frame, or that the threshold is the right definition of an edge.
if_wrong: Overlay that hides the image: the viewer cannot judge the edge.
A contour that is smooth and perfect: perhaps smoothed after the fact, or drawn from a model, not from the data.
Axis labelled px with unit-range ticks: pixel counts and normalised coordinates are being mixed.

terms.meaning: Deciding which pixels belong to the object and which to the background.
Intensity level that separates object from background; here a fixed fraction of the maximum.
The curve at the boundary of the segmented region.
A drawing on top of the original image, so that the data stay visible beneath the result.
A bar of known physical length drawn in the image to convert pixels to millimetres.

remember: Keep the original frame visible under the overlay.
A contour at level L of a Gaussian blob has half-width sigma sqrt(ln(1/L)).
Always draw a scale bar; always state the threshold.
One frame is an example, not a validation.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Grey levels show the camera frame, so position encodes the plane of the image and brightness the light intensity. The orange line encodes the detected contour at a chosen intensity level. The teal bar with its label gives the physical length, so the reader can convert distances. A grey frame with one saturated overlay colour keeps the two layers separate.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: A detection result is a claim about an image. The strongest check is to put the claim on the image: if the contour is on the edge of the visible feature, the claim is credible, and if not, the error is obvious. A numerical quality score would hide where the problem is. The scale bar connects pixels to the physical world so that the size can be judged.

understand.title: Read this reference render
understand.text: Q1: Does the contour match the edge? Yes at most places: it runs around the bright oval, but the line is ragged in several places, where noise crosses the threshold, with small loops and spurs. Q2: How big is the object? The 5 mm bar spans 0.5 to 0.8 in axis units, 0.3 units. The oval is about 0.72 units wide (x from -0.36 to +0.36) and 1.43 units long (y from -0.92 to +0.52): so about 12 mm by 24 mm. Q3: What is wrong with the axes? The label says px but the ticks run from -1 to 1: pixels would be integers up to a few hundred. Only the scale bar is reliable.

understand.title: The must-check list, explained
understand.text: Original frame visible and a legend of overlay colours: the grey frame under the line is the evidence, and the colour legend (the one overlay is the contour at the stated threshold) tells which line is which. Both are required, because an overlay without the frame cannot be checked and unnamed colours cannot be interpreted.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: An edge is defined by a threshold, and a different threshold gives a different edge; in the Gaussian example here, changing the level from 0.35 to 0.5 shrinks the width by about 19 percent, which is bigger than the pixel noise on the contour. A flame or glow has no sharp edge, so any contour is a convention. Contrast stretching (display range) changes how the edge looks. In this render the axes are labelled px but run from -1 to 1, so the labels cannot be used to measure; only the scale bar can.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: Show several thresholds as nested contours; plot intensity profiles across the edge with the threshold marked; show the segmentation mask next to the frame; give an error estimate from repeated frames.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add two more contours at levels 0.2 and 0.5 in lighter and darker orange, and a small intensity profile across the object with the threshold marked.

steps.title: Contour of a Gaussian blob at relative level L
steps.note: Half-width at the level L of the maximum. L = 0.35 gives 1.025 sigma; L = 0.5 gives 0.833 sigma.

steps.title: Threshold sensitivity of the width
steps.note: The apparent size depends on the definition of the edge: quote the threshold.

worked.title: Size from the scale bar and sensitivity to the threshold
worked.problem: The oval's half-width at L = 0.35 is 0.358 axis units, and the 5 mm bar spans 0.30 units. Find the width in mm. By how much would the width change if the threshold were 0.5?

solution.text: Ratio of widths at L = 0.5 and L = 0.35.

worked.answer: About 12 mm wide. A threshold of 0.5 would give 9.7 mm: a 19 percent change from a convention alone.

analyze.q: The contour is ragged at the edge. Is the ragged contour evidence of a bad algorithm or of a noisy image?
How would you decide on the threshold for a flame, which has no sharp edge?

evaluate.q: Is a good overlay on one frame enough to trust 10 000 frames?
evaluate.hint: What changes from frame to frame?

create: Draw three nested contours and a profile across the object.
Redraw the axes in millimetres using the calibration, and delete the pixel label.

checks.q: Why keep the original frame under the overlay?
checks.answer: So that the viewer can compare the contour with the visible edge.

checks.q: The 5 mm bar is 0.30 units and the object is 0.72 units wide. Width in mm?
A contour at level 0.2 and one at 0.5 differ in width by 52 percent of sigma. What do you do?
checks.answer: The ratio is 1.52: pick a physically motivated definition, state it, and report the width with the threshold range as an uncertainty.
